finding_problem: Recycling and street cleaning are two different services joined by 'and'. A respondent who is satisfied with one and dissatisfied with the other has no true answer on a single scale. Any midpoint answer or choice of one service cannot be told apart in the data.
evidence: 'the recycling services and street cleaning provided by your local council'

finding_problem: The stem assumes every respondent has these services from the local council and has had some experience of them. Some respondents may have a private or landlord arrangement, no recycling collection, or no idea who provides the service. For them the question does not apply, and there is no filter.
note: The finding also says respondents may have had no experience of the services (F1-P3's content); one finding matches one problem, so F1-P3 counts as not found.
evidence: 'provided by your local council'

finding_problem: The wording does not say whose finances count (own or household), which part of them (income, savings, debts, spending) or what 'current' covers (today, this month, this year). The respondent has to settle all three before judging, so answers can differ in meaning from one person to the next.
evidence: 'your current financial situation'

finding_problem: The stem gives no definition of 'vigorous' or 'moderate', so respondents may draw the line between them in different places, and some may treat the two as the same thing. On the web the definition has to be on screen with the question, and the stem has none.
evidence: 'vigorous physical activity and moderate physical activity'

finding_problem: The stem does not say whether activity at paid work, housework, getting around or in free time counts. Respondents who have physically active jobs or do heavy housework could include it or leave it out, and the estimate would shift accordingly.
evidence: 'physical activity' (no setting named) and 'In a typical week'

finding_problem: The item asks about two different intensities of activity and requires one total. A respondent may do a lot of one kind and little of the other, and the total hides this. The two hours-per-week quantities can no longer be analysed separately.
evidence: 'vigorous physical activity and moderate physical activity combined'

finding_problem: Respondents must decide what a 'typical' week is, estimate hours for two kinds of activity and add them in their heads. This is harder for people whose weeks vary, for example because of shift work, seasons or irregular exercise. Short bouts spread across the week are also hard to recall and total up.
evidence: 'In a typical week, how many hours ... combined'

finding_problem: The opening states as fact that pressure on public services is growing, and the tag 'don't you think' invites a yes. The closing clause frames immigrants as a possible burden. Together these make agreement the expected answer and supply a reason for it before the respondent has formed a view.
evidence: 'Given the growing pressure on public services, don't you think that the government should do more' and 'particularly those who may not contribute to the economy'

finding_problem: The stem is a negative interrogative. It also stacks an introductory clause, a main clause and a trailing qualifier in one sentence. Respondents must keep all of it in mind, and with a negative question it is unclear what 'agree' means.
evidence: 'don't you think that the government should do more to reduce the number of immigrants coming to this country, particularly those who may not contribute to the economy'

finding_problem: The item asks about reducing immigration in general and about reducing it for one subgroup. A respondent who wants fewer non-contributing immigrants but not fewer immigrants overall, or the reverse, has no accurate answer. 'Do more' and 'reduce the number' also add a policy-effort judgment to a judgment about the level.
evidence: 'reduce the number of immigrants coming to this country, particularly those who may not contribute to the economy'

finding_problem: 'Contribute to the economy' can mean paid work, paying tax, running a business, unpaid care or spending. 'May not' also leaves open whether it means now or in future. Respondents will read the group differently. 'Immigrants' may likewise be read as including or excluding refugees, students or long-settled residents.
evidence: 'those who may not contribute to the economy'

finding_problem: 'Do more' compares against current government action that many respondents may not know, and no policy, group or time frame is named. Respondents may answer about the current level of immigration, about government effort, or about a general feeling. These are different things.
evidence: 'the government should do more to reduce the number of immigrants'

finding_problem: A one-sided statement is open to acquiescence, and the leading wording adds to the pull toward agreeing. A direct question about the preferred level of immigration would ask for the same judgment without requiring respondents to convert it into agreement.
evidence: Strongly agree to Strongly disagree, attached to a single statement worded in one direction

finding_problem: The question assumes every respondent has an employer and a work contract. Retired people, students, unemployed people, full-time carers and many self-employed people have no terms of employment to rate. They must skip, guess or pick a scale point that is not true for them. Respondents with more than one job also do not know which job to rate.
evidence: 'your terms of employment' asked of 'Adults in the general population' with no filter and no not-applicable option

finding_problem: This is a contract-style phrase. Some respondents will read it narrowly as pay, hours and holidays in their contract. Others will read it as the job in general, the workplace or their manager. The answer then rests on different content for different people.
evidence: 'terms of employment'

finding_problem: The scale has three positive points and two negative points, so it is not balanced, and there is no neutral middle point. 'Completely' and 'very' are hard to tell apart, and the order of 'very' and 'fairly' depends on how each respondent reads these intensity words. Respondents who are neither satisfied nor dissatisfied have no true option, and no 'not applicable' option is offered (see the finding on presupposition).
evidence: 'Completely satisfied / Very satisfied / Fairly satisfied / Not very satisfied / Not at all satisfied'

finding_problem: Every adult respondent reaches Q1, so the question reaches people it does not apply to, and no route leads non-employees to a suitable next question. A screening question and a skip are needed before Q1 in the full instrument.
evidence: Q1 is the only item, with no screening question before it and no routing for people who are not employees

finding_problem: To answer, the respondent may have to find out what other household members receive, add several incomes together, convert weekly, annual or irregular pay into a monthly figure, and work out a before-tax figure when they may only know what is paid into their account. Each of these steps can produce a wrong total or a mixed basis (some before tax, some after).
note: Borderline: the finding is about the respondent having to find out and add up what other household members receive, not about household income being unidentifiable as such.
evidence: 'total monthly income from all sources, before tax and deductions' for the household

finding_problem: The item does not say who counts as part of the household (for example adult children, lodgers, or relatives who share only some costs). It also does not say which month is meant (last month, a usual month, or an average), which matters when income varies. On the web there is no interviewer to explain, so any definition must be in the visible question text. The household definition should match the benchmark source the analyst will compare against, which the brief does not name.
evidence: 'household's' and 'monthly'

finding_problem: 'All sources' does not tell the respondent whether benefits, pensions, gifts from family, savings withdrawals, loans or one-off payments count. 'Deductions' is a payroll term whose scope (pension contributions, loan repayments, other items) is not clear to everyone. Respondents may therefore include different things.
evidence: 'from all sources' and 'before tax and deductions'

finding_problem: The stem asks about two destinations, work and essential services, and the services are themselves several things. A respondent who finds the trip to work easy but the trip to a clinic hard has no single true answer and must average or pick one part. The analyst cannot tell which part the answer describes.
evidence: 'get to work and to access essential services such as healthcare'

finding_problem: The stem assumes the respondent has a job they travel to. Retired people, unemployed people, full-time carers and people who work from home do not fit. The brief gives no filter, so these respondents must guess, skip or answer about something else.
evidence: 'get to work'

finding_problem: 'Essential services' has no fixed meaning, and one example does not say which others count. 'Access' can mean physically travelling there, getting an appointment, affording it or being eligible. Respondents may therefore answer about different things.
evidence: 'access essential services such as healthcare'

finding_problem: The stem does not say whether difficulty means distance, travel time, cost, lack of transport or something else. It does not say which way of travelling to think of, or whether to think of a usual trip or the worst one. Respondents will fill these gaps differently. The analyst must decide which dimension and reference period the study needs.
evidence: 'How easy or difficult is it' with no time frame, no way of travelling and no dimension of difficulty

finding_problem: A respondent who does not travel to work, or who has not needed healthcare, has no true option on the scale shown. A respondent whose answers differ between work and services also has no true option. The in-between options were not shown, so a midpoint could not be checked.
evidence: 'a scale running from Very easy to Very difficult' with no 'does not apply' option visible

finding_problem: The term has no definition on screen. Respondents can differ on whether messaging apps, video-sharing sites, forums or workplace tools count, so the same hours could be reported or left out differently. 'Platforms' is also a technical word that not everyone uses for these services. The brief does not say which services the analyst wants counted, so that decision has to come from the analyst.
evidence: 'social media platforms'

finding_problem: Respondents must recall many short sessions across several apps and devices, add them up, and convert the total to hours. Use that is spread through the day or runs in the background is hard to total. Respondents are likely to fall back on a guess or a stereotype of their own use.
evidence: 'Roughly how many hours per week do you spend on social media platforms?'

finding_problem: The statement joins a view about how severe punishment should be with a view about longer prison sentences. A respondent who wants severe punishment but through other means, or who does not accept longer sentences, has no true answer on one agree-disagree scale. The 'even if' clause also assumes that severe punishment means longer prison terms.
evidence: 'deserve to be punished severely, even if this means longer prison sentences'

finding_problem: Respondents may picture very different crimes (for example violent crime, fraud, drug offences) and different meanings of 'severely'. The answers then reflect different private reference points rather than one common object. Choosing which crimes to name, or whether to leave the term broad, narrows or changes the construct and is the analyst's decision.
evidence: 'serious crimes' and 'punished severely'

finding_problem: Only the punitive side is stated and there is no item keyed the other way, so acquiescence would inflate agreement and cannot be separated from the attitude. A construct-specific question about how severe punishment should be could do the same job without a statement to accept or reject.
evidence: 'To what extent do you agree or disagree?' after a single one-directional statement

finding_problem: The stem asks about two situations at once. A respondent who feels safe in daylight but uneasy at night has no single true answer and must pick one, average the two, or answer for only one part. The result cannot be read as either time of day.
evidence: 'during the day and after dark'

finding_problem: The stem does not say how large 'your neighbourhood' is. It could mean the street, the block, or a wider district. It also does not say whether it means being at home or walking outside, or what the respondent should be safe from, such as crime, traffic or something else. Respondents will fill these gaps differently.
evidence: 'safe in your neighbourhood'

finding_problem: The question assumes every respondent needed, and tried to get, an appointment in the past 12 months. Respondents who did not need one, or who needed one but never tried to book, have no true answer on an easy-to-difficult scale. They may skip, guess, or pick a middle point, and that would mix non-users into the ratings.
evidence: 'when you needed one' with no filter before the item and no not-applicable option shown

finding_problem: The phrase covers many kinds of provider (for example doctor, nurse, dentist, specialist, therapist, pharmacist). It also does not say whether a phone, video or walk-in contact counts as an appointment. Respondents will include different providers and contacts, and one who found a doctor easy but a specialist hard has no single true answer. The scope of 'healthcare professional' depends on what the analyst wants to measure, which the brief does not say.
evidence: 'a healthcare professional'

finding_problem: A 12-month period can cover several appointments with different levels of difficulty. The respondent must remember them and average them into one rating, or may base the answer on the most recent or most memorable one. Different respondents will use different strategies.
evidence: 'In the past 12 months, how easy has it been'

finding_problem: The first sentence states a claim as fact and appeals to research. It tells respondents what answer is expected before they judge for themselves, so high importance is favoured. This review cannot check whether the claim is true, but a question should not carry it as a premise.
evidence: 'Research consistently shows that children benefit from having a parent at home in the early years.'

finding_problem: The item changes its object from 'a parent' to 'mothers', so the question bundles gender with the at-home arrangement. A respondent who thinks it matters that a parent is home, but not that it is the mother, has no accurate answer. Whether the intended construct is parental care or mothers' roles is not stated in the brief.
note: Same feature (the shift from 'a parent' to 'mothers') but framed as bundling gender with the at-home arrangement (one_thing), not as sensitivity.
evidence: The lead-in says 'a parent at home', but the question asks 'that mothers stay at home'.

finding_problem: The phrase does not say whether it means full time, or whether a mother who works part time or from home counts. Respondents may read it differently and answer different questions. The analyst must decide which meaning is intended.
evidence: 'stay at home to look after their children'

finding_problem: The first phrase asks for an overall view of life. The second narrows it to the present moment. Respondents may answer from today's mood or from a longer stretch of their life, and the brief does not say which time frame the analyst intends.
evidence: 'Taking everything into account' together with 'at this moment'

finding_problem: The stem asks about two qualities joined by 'and'. A respondent who finds childcare easy to get but too costly, or the reverse, has no true answer on a single satisfaction scale. Any answer also mixes two judgments, so it cannot be read as either one.
evidence: 'availability and affordability of childcare services'

finding_problem: The stem assumes the respondent knows enough about local childcare to judge it. Adults with no children, or whose children no longer need care, may have no basis for an answer. They must either guess, pick a midpoint they do not mean, or leave the item. Whether the analyst wants the views of all adults or only those with experience is not stated in the brief.
note: Borderline between exact and approximate: framed as respondents lacking a basis to judge childcare (adults with no children), where the known problem says the question assumes a need for childcare.
evidence: 'How satisfied are you with ... childcare services in your area?' asked of 'Adults in the general population' with no filter or not-applicable option

finding_problem: The term can be read as formal paid provision, such as nurseries or paid carers. It can also be read to include care by grandparents or other relatives, or after-school care. Which meaning a respondent picks changes what they judge. The analyst must decide which kinds of care the item is meant to cover.
evidence: 'childcare services'

finding_problem: 'Area' has no fixed size. Respondents may think of their street, their town or a wider region, and may judge different sets of providers. Where it is meant to apply, such as near home or near work, is also left open.
evidence: 'in your area'

finding_problem: The lead-in states two contested claims as fact and says what the respondent is expected to value. Respondents who want to appear responsible, or who feel they should have acted, may report more change than they made, and those who disagree with the claims may be pushed to react to them. The shifts would come from the framing, not from behaviour.
evidence: 'Considering the urgent need to address climate change and the fact that individual actions collectively make a significant difference'

finding_problem: This is a technical or metaphorical term, and the item gives no definition. Some respondents may read it as energy use only, others as all environmental harm, and others may not know it. The web mode allows the definition to sit in the question text.
evidence: 'personal carbon footprint'

finding_problem: 'Daily habits' covers many different behaviours, such as travel, food, home energy and shopping. A respondent who changed one area but not another has no clear answer. To pick one position on the scale, the respondent must recall changes across all areas, add them up, and decide which count as done 'specifically' for this reason. The brief names no construct, so the domains that matter are for the analyst to choose.
evidence: 'changes to your daily habits'

finding_problem: The question asks about change over the past year. Someone who already lived in a low-carbon way before that year, and so made no recent change, has no true option: 'Not at all' would suggest they do nothing. The in-between options were not shown, so they could not be checked.
evidence: Response options 'A great deal' to 'Not at all'

finding_problem: 'Community organisation' has no shared boundary. Respondents may differ on whether a place of worship, sports club, school parents' group, trade union or national charity counts. 'Work' may also be read as a job-like task, so helping at a one-off event could be left out. The brief does not say which organisations the analyst wants counted.
evidence: 'voluntary or unpaid work for a community organisation'

finding_problem: A 'time' is not defined. A weekly volunteer might count each session, count each week, or count the whole year as one ongoing commitment, and a one-off event might count as one. 'Past year' could also mean the last 12 months or the calendar year.
note: The finding's main point is that a 'time' is undefined; its last sentence says 'past year' could mean the last 12 months or the calendar year, which is F16-P3.
evidence: 'How many times in the past year'

finding_problem: The respondent must recall and count episodes over 12 months. Regular volunteers have to multiply or estimate, and occasional volunteers may forget one-off events. The task is hard at the retrieval stage in different ways for these two groups.
evidence: 'How many times in the past year' combined with a top option of 'More than 10 times'

finding_problem: The stem asks how adequate the space is, which invites an answer such as 'very adequate' or 'not at all adequate'. The options instead measure whether there is too much or too little space. A respondent with plenty of space may think 'adequate' fits well but find no matching option, or may be unsure how 'adequate' maps onto 'too much'. The stem and the scale ask different questions.
evidence: 'How adequate is the amount of space' paired with options running from 'Far too much space' to 'Far too little space'

finding_problem: The question does not say which space counts: rooms inside, storage, a garden, balcony or other outdoor areas. It does not say which needs count: sleeping, privacy, working or studying at home, hosting, storage. Respondents may fill these gaps differently, so the same housing situation could get different answers. The analyst must decide what the space construct covers, and this review cannot decide it.
evidence: 'the amount of space in the home' and 'the needs of your household'

finding_problem: The stem asks about two topics with one answer. A respondent who argues often about money but never about children has no true single answer. Anyone who answers has to average the two topics in their head, and the analyst cannot tell which topic drove the answer.
evidence: 'argue about money and about how to raise your children'

finding_problem: The stem assumes every respondent has a partner and children they are raising. Adults in the general population include people with no partner and people with no children, so the question does not apply to them. The wording also assumes that arguments happen at all.
evidence: 'you and your partner' and 'your children'

finding_problem: The stem gives no reference period, so each respondent picks their own: the past week, the past year, or the whole relationship. Answers are then not comparable. The brief gives no reference period, so its length is the analyst's choice.
evidence: 'How often do you...' with no time frame

finding_problem: No option is offered for people with no partner or no children. They must choose 'Never', which is untrue for them and mixes them with partnered respondents who do not argue. This overlaps with the presupposition finding: a filter question or a 'does not apply' option would each solve it, and the analyst decides which.
evidence: 'a scale running from Very often to Never'

finding_problem: Nothing sends people without a partner, or without children, past Q1. Every adult in the general population would reach an item that applies only to some of them. In web mode no interviewer can skip or clarify it.
evidence: Q1 is the only item pasted and no screening question comes before it

finding_problem: The opening clause states as fact that there were scandals and links them to the trust judgment. This pushes respondents toward low trust and supplies the mood and the standard of comparison for the answer.
evidence: Given the recent scandals in government

finding_problem: The question assumes every respondent knows of these scandals and accepts that they happened. Respondents who know of none, or who dispute the label 'scandals', cannot answer on the terms given. The brief does not say which events are meant.
evidence: the recent scandals in government

finding_problem: It is not clear whose trust is being asked about: national, regional or local politicians, the governing party, or all of them. Respondents must choose their own referent and may differ, and they must average across many people to answer. The analyst should choose the level that matches the research aim, which the brief does not state.
evidence: politicians

finding_problem: One sentence holds the question, a 'not including' exclusion list, a 'but including' inclusion list and a time frame. The respondent has to keep both lists in mind before reaching the end, and the negated exclusion adds load. Some respondents will lose part of the rule and answer on their own idea of leisure.
evidence: not including time spent on domestic tasks, caring responsibilities, or personal grooming, but including any time spent on hobbies, socialising, watching television, reading, or using the internet for personal enjoyment

finding_problem: The respondent must recall several separate activities, estimate time for each, add them up, and average over days that may differ. Activities that overlap, such as television on while doing chores or internet use at work, make the sum harder to judge. Anyone whose weekdays vary has no 'typical' day to retrieve.
evidence: On a typical weekday, approximately how many hours do you spend on leisure activities ... hobbies, socialising, watching television, reading, or using the internet

finding_problem: These are formal terms and may not be read the same way by everyone. 'Caring responsibilities' may be taken to mean only care for someone ill or dependent, so playing with one's own child could be counted as leisure by some and as care by others. 'Domestic tasks' may or may not include cooking, gardening or shopping.
evidence: domestic tasks, caring responsibilities, or personal grooming

finding_problem: The lists do not say how to treat activities that fall between categories, such as sport or exercise, resting or doing nothing, religious or community activity, or cooking or gardening done for pleasure. Respondents will draw the boundary differently, so totals are not comparable. Which of these belong in the construct is the analyst's decision.
note: Matched to this finding (activities between categories) rather than to the plain_words finding on the exclusion terms, because one finding matches one problem.
evidence: leisure activities

finding_problem: 'Fruit' is read differently by different people: fresh only, or also dried, tinned or frozen fruit, fruit in a smoothie, or fruit cooked into a dish. The exclusion names only juice, so the other forms are left to each respondent. Which forms count is the analyst's decision, and the brief does not say.
evidence: fruit, excluding drinking juice

finding_problem: The stem gives no time frame, so each respondent picks their own period, such as last week, a typical week or the current season. Fruit eating can vary by season and by week. The unit 'times' is also undefined: it could mean separate eating occasions or pieces of fruit, so someone who eats two apples at once could answer either way. Which period fits depends on what the estimate is for, and the brief does not say.
evidence: 'How often do you eat fruit' with the top option 'Three times or more a day'

finding_problem: The item does not say which parts of life to consider (for example work, money, health, family), so respondents could each pick different parts or average over them. 'Nowadays' gives no clear time frame, so it is unclear whether the answer is about this week, this year or recent years. The brief names no construct or reference period, so the analyst must decide how narrow the item should be.
evidence: 'over your life in general nowadays'
